strengths: State-of-the-art empirical performance across an extensive and diverse suite of seven major reward model benchmarks (RewardBench v1 & v2, PPE Preference & Correctness, RMB, RM-Bench, and JudgeBench), with the 8B model outperforming much larger models (e.g., 70B) and frontier generative judges.

Significant open-source resource contribution, including the massive SynPref-40M preference dataset and eight reward models spanning 0.6B to 8B parameters across multiple architectures (Llama-3.1/3.2 and Qwen3).
A well-designed, scalable two-stage curation pipeline integrating human verification, attribute generation, error-driven adaptive retrieval, and consistency-based filtering.

Comprehensive and informative ablation studies demonstrating that scaling uncurated preference data plateaus quickly, whereas rigorous human-guided curation enables genuine scaling and effective error correction.
Robustness and fine-grained evaluations covering Best-of-N scaling dynamics, resistance to style and length biases (RM-Bench), and objective reasoning capabilities.
weaknesses: Lack of end-to-end downstream policy optimization experiments (e.g., training a policy model with PPO, REINFORCE, or Best-of-N against benchmarks like AlpacaEval 2 or Arena-Hard) to definitively verify that the benchmark gains translate to superior downstream policy alignment without reward hacking.

Certain details regarding the human annotation process remain vague, such as the exact volume of human-verified pairs ($D_{gold}$ vs. $D_{silver}$), inter-annotator agreement metrics, annotator demographics, and compensation.

The label-flipping heuristic ('recycling' discarded pairs by inverting chosen and rejected responses) yields empirical gains but lacks a rigorous theoretical justification, which may risk reinforcing systematic biases or label noise under certain conditions.
High computational and monetary barrier to reproduce the full curation pipeline from scratch due to reliance on extensive commercial frontier LLM APIs and heavy human-in-the-loop annotation.

strengths: State-of-the-art empirical performance: The resulting Skywork-Reward-V2 models (particularly the 8B variants) outperform all prior open reward models (including 70B scale models like Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B and INF-ORM-Llama3.1-70B) across seven comprehensive and challenging benchmarks, including RewardBench v2, PPE, RMB, and RM-Bench.

Principled and effective data curation pipeline: The paper presents a well-structured two-stage human-AI synergistic framework that combines error-driven adaptive retrieval, human-in-the-loop verification, and RM consistency filtering, effectively addressing the noise and saturation issues inherent in uncurated web-scale preference datasets.

Insightful ablation experiments: The authors provide compelling ablations dissecting data quantity versus quality, demonstrating that simply scaling uncurated data yields negligible benefits, whereas curated subsets—even at 1.8% volume—can surpass prior state-of-the-art models.

High practical impact and open resources: Releasing a diverse suite of eight reward models ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters across multiple architectures (Llama 3.1/3.2, Qwen3) provides immense value and accessibility to the open-source post-training and RLHF community.

Thorough evaluation beyond simple pairwise accuracy: Evaluation includes Best-of-N scaling curves, resistance to stylistic biases (RM-Bench), objective correctness (PPE Correctness, JudgeBench), and safety.
weaknesses: Lack of online policy training evaluation: While Best-of-N scaling and correlations with downstream benchmarks are thoroughly reported, the paper does not show actual downstream policy optimization experiments (e.g., PPO or online RLHF) using Skywork-Reward-V2 to directly confirm policy improvements.

Heuristic nature of label flipping: The 'recycling' of 14 million discarded pairs via simple label flipping is justified purely empirically; a deeper error analysis is needed to determine whether flipped pairs contain ambiguous or inherently low-quality text that could cause reward hacking.

Limited quantitative analysis of human annotation reliability: Although human curation is identified as critical, the paper lacks detailed inter-annotator agreement metrics (e.g., Fleiss' or Cohen's kappa) and exact human labor/cost statistics across the iterative curation stages.

strengths: State-of-the-art empirical performance: The Skywork-Reward-V2 models (ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters) consistently outperform substantially larger models (e.g., 70B parameter models and leading proprietary LLM judges) across seven major reward modeling benchmarks, establishing a strong new open-weight baseline.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation suite: Instead of relying solely on RewardBench (which is prone to saturation and weak correlation with real task performance), the authors evaluate across diverse dimensions including objective correctness (PPE Correctness, JudgeBench), style-bias robustness (RM-Bench), Best-of-N scaling (RMB, PPE), and fine-grained instruction following (RewardBench v2).

Effective curation framework: The two-stage human-AI synergistic pipeline—combining structured attribute-guided human verification with error-driven adaptive retrieval and consistency-based filtering—provides a well-motivated and scalable methodology for curating tens of millions of preference pairs.

Insightful ablation experiments: The paper presents valuable findings regarding preference data scaling, notably showing that uncurated preference data quickly saturates, that error-driven adaptive retrieval meaningfully boosts LLM annotation quality, and that structured guidelines and tool access substantially elevate human annotation performance.
weaknesses: Lack of downstream policy optimization: Although the paper emphasizes the role of reward models in RLHF pipelines, the evaluation is restricted to offline reward benchmarks and Best-of-N sampling; it lacks downstream online RL training (e.g., PPO or REINFORCE-style policy optimization) to verify whether these gains translate directly into improved policy behavior.

Under-specified human annotation details: Crucial metadata regarding the human-in-the-loop stage is missing from the main body, such as the total number of human annotators, their compensation/demographics, training protocol duration, and formal inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Cohen's or Fleiss' kappa).

Heuristic nature of flipping discarded pairs: Recycling discarded preference pairs by simply inverting chosen and rejected labels is acknowledged as an empirical heuristic without rigorous safety or tie checks, which could introduce noisy or degenerate preference signals in cases where both responses are flawed or nearly identical.

High computational requirement: Filtering tens of millions of samples and training large RM suites with extensive contexts (16K tokens) on clusters of 64× H800 GPUs presents a reproducibility barrier for standard academic research environments.

strengths: Substantial empirical contribution: The Skywork-Reward-V2 models achieve state-of-the-art results across seven established reward modeling benchmarks, remarkably enabling 8B and even 1.7B-4B models to outperform much larger 70B open reward models and competitive LLM-as-a-judge systems.

Principled and effective human-AI synergistic curation pipeline: The two-stage framework sensibly balances high-quality human verification (augmented by structured preference attributes and tool use) with scalable LLM annotation via error-driven adaptive retrieval and dual-RM consistency filtering.

Insightful data-centric findings: The paper convincingly demonstrates that scaling uncurated preference data provides negligible gains, whereas curated scaling succeeds. The observation and empirical verification that inverted/discarded pairs can be reliably recycled by flipping preference labels offer high practical value.

Extensive and rigorous evaluation: The authors evaluate on a multi-dimensional benchmark suite (addressing known saturation and flaws of RewardBench v1), test for stylistic robustness, provide Best-of-N scaling trajectories, and validate downstream RLHF improvements on instruction-following models.

Thorough ablations: The manuscript includes detailed ablations isolating the impact of human curation, attribute prompting, tool assistance, adaptive retrieval, and pure LLM filtering versus human-guided filtering.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The underlying modeling approach relies entirely on the standard pointwise Bradley-Terry loss and standard dense transformer backbones; the contribution is predominantly data-engineering and curation methodology rather than new learning algorithms.

Heavy dependency on proprietary frontier models: The data curation and preference-attribute generation rely heavily on high-end commercial LLM APIs (e.g., Claude 3.5/3.7, GPT-4o, OpenAI o-series, Gemini 2.5 Pro), making the full curation pipeline challenging and costly to reproduce independently without identical API behavior.

Decontamination complexities at scale: Although 13-gram deduplication and LLM verification checks are applied, ensuring absolute decontamination across a heterogeneous 40M-pair web-scraped pool against diverse evaluation benchmarks remains difficult, and subtle distribution leakage into synthetic responses cannot be fully eliminated.

strengths: State-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks: The resulting Skywork-Reward-V2 models (ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters) consistently outperform prior open-source reward models, including much larger 70B models and recent generative reward models, across seven comprehensive RM benchmarks.

Well-designed and principled data curation methodology: The proposed two-stage human-AI synergistic curation framework—integrating error-driven adaptive retrieval, human-guided in-context few-shot LLM judging, and dual-RM consistency filtering/recycling—provides a practical and effective blueprint for scaling preference data.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation and ablations: The authors provide thorough experiments, including cross-benchmark correlation analysis, ablations demonstrating that data curation/correction significantly outperforms naive data scaling, component-wise ablations of human/LLM contributions, and validation on downstream policy optimization (RLHF).

Practical utility and budgeting insights: The paper offers valuable engineering insights for practitioners, including cost-performance budgeting breakdowns and analysis on handling intransitive/noisy preferences in large-scale datasets.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on closed frontier models: The curation pipeline relies heavily on high-end proprietary LLMs (such as GPT-4o, Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.5 Pro) with search and tool-use capabilities for preference attribute extraction and silver labeling, creating cost and reproducibility hurdles for researchers without equivalent API access.

Potential bias in human verification: Stage 1 human annotations and guidelines involved fewer than 20 annotators, including the paper's authors. Given the small annotator pool and involvement of authors, there is potential for unintended subjective bias or implicit alignment towards specific benchmark characteristics.

Risk of benchmark leakage despite decontamination: Although the authors describe 13-gram and semantic decontamination checks across prompts and completions, sourcing from 40+ public Hugging Face datasets (which frequently scrape or overlap with standard evaluation suites) presents persistent risks of paraphrased benchmark contamination.

Limited modeling novelty: From a machine learning modeling perspective, the approach uses standard Bradley-Terry sequence classifiers without novel loss formulations or architectural advances, with the primary novelty lying in the data curation pipeline and engineering.

strengths: Outstanding empirical results across an extensive benchmark suite: The resulting Skywork-Reward-V2 models (ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters) consistently outperform substantially larger open models (e.g., 70B baselines like INF-ORM and Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B) as well as frontier generative judges across seven modern RM benchmarks, including RewardBench v2, RMB, RM-Bench, and PPE.

Principled and scalable data curation framework: The two-stage curation pipeline smartly combines high-leverage human verification on error-prone/hard subsets with scalable, human-guided LLM annotation and dual-RM consistency filtering, offering practical insights into data-centric RLHF.

Insightful ablations on preference data scaling and quality: The paper clearly illustrates the saturation and failure of scaling uncurated/raw preference data versus curated data, demonstrating that curating a tiny fraction (1.8%) of high-quality data can match or exceed prior state-of-the-art 70B models.

Validation beyond static proxy benchmarks: In addition to pairwise classification benchmarks, the authors evaluate Best-of-N scaling curves, resistance to stylistic biases, and downstream RLHF policy optimization on ArenaHard, MT-Bench, and WildBench, ensuring the RM improvements translate to actual generative performance.
weaknesses: High pipeline complexity and resource demands: The overall pipeline involves multiple iterations of model training, embedding-based adaptive retrieval, human annotation using external web tools, and calls to numerous frontier proprietary and open LLMs. This makes exact end-to-end replication extremely resource-intensive for academic and resource-constrained research groups.

Potential risk of subtle distribution overlap: Although the authors implemented strict 13-gram prompt decontamination and frontier LLM semantic filtering, aggregating from over 40 public datasets carries inherent risks of prompt style or domain overlap with popular benchmark distributions.

Reliance on the transitive Bradley-Terry framework: While the data curation addresses noisy and intransitive pairs via consistency checks and label flipping, collapsing diverse, subjective human preferences into a single scalar Bradley-Terry score fundamentally limits the modeling of conflicting or multi-objective preferences.
